facts.title: Born in a Bomb's Fire
facts.text: Einsteinium was discovered in December 1952 in the radioactive debris of the first thermonuclear (hydrogen) bomb test, code-named 'Ivy Mike,' detonated over Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific. The intense neutron flux let uranium nuclei swallow many neutrons at once, building up to element 99 before beta decay raised the proton count. Because the work was tied to a classified weapons test, the discovery was kept secret and not published until 1955.

facts.title: Named for Einstein
facts.text: The element honors Albert Einstein, who was still alive when it was discovered but died in April 1955, shortly before the naming was made public. The team at the University of California, Berkeley, led by Albert Ghiorso, proposed the name; einsteinium and its neighbor fermium (element 100, for Enrico Fermi) were named for giants of physics. Einstein himself reportedly never knew an element had been named after him.

facts.title: It Glows in the Dark
facts.text: Einsteinium is so intensely radioactive that visible quantities glow with a soft blue light, caused by the energy released as its own radiation excites the surrounding air and material. This self-luminescence is a direct, eerie demonstration of just how much energy these unstable nuclei pour out. The same radioactivity heats the metal noticeably above room temperature.

facts.title: A Metal That Cooks Itself
facts.text: The decay of einsteinium-253 releases roughly 1,000 watts of heat per gram, enough to make a sample warm to the touch and to slowly damage the very crystal it forms. This intense self-heating, combined with radiation, makes the metal's properties extraordinarily hard to measure. Scientists must race against the clock because the material literally destroys itself from the inside.

facts.title: You Can't Find It in Nature
facts.text: Einsteinium does not occur naturally on Earth in any meaningful amount; every atom that exists has been made artificially in reactors or accelerators. Its longest-lived isotope, einsteinium-252, has a half-life of only about 472 days, far too short to have survived since the planet formed. Any primordial einsteinium vanished billions of years ago.

facts.title: Made by the Microgram
facts.text: Einsteinium is among the rarest synthesized elements: it is produced at the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee, and only fractions of a milligram are made per year. A typical research sample might contain just a few micrograms or even nanograms. This scarcity means most experiments use vanishingly small amounts handled with extreme care.

facts.title: The Bridge to Heavier Elements
facts.text: Einsteinium served as a crucial stepping stone in the hunt for new elements: bombarding an einsteinium target with alpha particles led to the 1955 discovery of mendelevium, element 101. Because einsteinium can be made in (barely) weighable quantities, it remains one of the heaviest elements usable as a target for creating even heavier ones. It is, in effect, a launchpad deeper into the periodic table.

facts.title: A Surprisingly Light Metal
facts.text: Despite sitting among the heavy actinides, einsteinium metal has a relatively low density of about 8.84 grams per cubic centimeter and a face-centered cubic crystal structure. Studies suggest its outer electrons are slightly more 'free' than in its neighbors, hinting at unusual bonding behavior at the edge of the actinide series. These quirks make it a valuable probe of how electron shells behave under extreme nuclear conditions.

facts.title: Chemistry Caught on Camera
facts.text: In 2021, scientists at Berkeley Lab and partner institutions performed some of the first detailed chemical bonding studies on einsteinium, using less than 250 nanograms of the element. They measured its bond distances and absorption behavior, revealing subtle departures from the trends seen in lighter actinides. The experiment was a tour de force, since the sample was decaying and damaging its container throughout the work.

facts.title: No Job, No Biology
facts.text: Einsteinium has no biological role whatsoever and is not part of any living organism; it exists purely as a tool for fundamental research. Because of its fierce radioactivity, it has no commercial or industrial applications and is studied only in specialized laboratories. Its entire reason for existing, from a human standpoint, is to help us understand the heaviest reaches of matter.
